36.text:
Smartphones, video calls and messaging apps have become part of nearly every friendship and family, and technology has changed how people relate to one another. This essay will explain two key ways in which technology affects relationships: by keeping people in touch across distance and by changing the quality of the time they spend together.

First and foremost, technology helps people to stay in touch and to form new connections. Video calls and messages connect families and friends across distances, and migrants and students abroad can speak to their relatives every day. A grandmother who watches her grandchildren's school play by video call from another country, for example, feels part of their lives. Social networks help people to find others who share their interests or circumstances, such as patients with a rare illness, and online communities can offer support to those who feel isolated in their own neighbourhood. Many friendships that would once have faded can now continue for years.

In addition, technology can weaken the quality of time together. Phones at the dinner table, constant notifications and the habit of checking messages reduce attention, so people may be in the same room without really listening to each other. Online communication can also be shallow, and conflicts can grow when tone is misunderstood in text. Online bullying and the pressure to display a perfect life on social media can harm self-esteem, especially among young people. However, these problems are not inevitable. Families can agree on phone-free meals, and friends can use messaging to arrange meetings in person. Relationships benefit when technology is used to add to face-to-face contact, not to replace it.

To sum up, technology affects relationships in both helpful and harmful ways, and its effect depends on how people choose to use it. For these reasons, it should be used thoughtfully.

45.text:
Hospitals, schools and charities rely on people who give their time without payment, and opinions differ on whether volunteering mainly benefits society or primarily benefits the volunteers. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that volunteering benefits society. Volunteers provide help that public services cannot always afford, from tutoring to care for older people, and many charities could not survive without them. A retired teacher who helps children to read after school, for example, offers support that the school could not pay for. Volunteering also builds community, since people who work together on a common cause meet neighbours they would not otherwise know and develop trust. In emergencies, from floods to pandemics, volunteers have often made the difference between a coordinated response and chaos. The work also shows that people care about each other beyond family ties.

On the other hand, others point out that volunteers themselves gain a great deal. They learn skills such as organising, communicating and teamwork, which may help them to find paid work, and they gain friendships, confidence and a sense of purpose. For young people, volunteering can provide experience that improves a career application, and for retired people it can reduce loneliness. A retired teacher who helps children to read, for instance, finds new purpose herself. Some critics suggest that this self-interest means volunteering is not truly selfless, although such motives do not reduce the value of the help given.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that volunteering benefits both society and the volunteer, and that this mutual benefit is the reason why it works so well.

Tình nguyện viên giúp mà dịch vụ công không đủ tiền (kèm cặp, chăm người già); nhiều tổ chức từ thiện không sống nổi nếu thiếu họ. Ví dụ giáo viên về hưu giúp trẻ đọc sau giờ học. Xây dựng cộng đồng: gặp hàng xóm, tin tưởng; trong khẩn cấp (lũ, đại dịch) tình nguyện viên tạo khác biệt giữa ứng phó phối hợp và hỗn loạn.

Học kỹ năng (tổ chức, giao tiếp, làm việc nhóm) có thể giúp tìm việc; bạn bè, tự tin, ý nghĩa; người trẻ có kinh nghiệm cải thiện hồ sơ, người về hưu bớt cô đơn; giáo viên về hưu tìm thấy mục đích mới. Một số chỉ trích: không hoàn toàn vị tha, nhưng động cơ này không giảm giá trị sự giúp đỡ.
Có lợi cho cả hai và chính sự hỗ tương này là lý do tình nguyện hiệu quả.

81.text:
Many owners treat their dogs and cats as part of the household, and some people say that pets are as important as family members. I disagree with this view, since pets give companionship and joy but cannot replace human family members, although their value should not be dismissed.

To begin with, pets give companionship and joy but cannot replace human family members. They reduce loneliness and encourage exercise and responsibility, yet they cannot offer the shared history, conversation and mutual obligations that bind a family. A widow whose dog greets her every day, for example, feels less alone, but the dog cannot replace the conversation of a relative or understand her worries. Family members support one another through illness, financial difficulty and important decisions, and they share memories that stretch over generations. A pet, however loved, does not take part in these exchanges in the same way. Humans also have rights and a moral status that animals, though deserving of kindness, do not share to the same degree.

Furthermore, treating pets as equal to relatives can lead to difficult choices. If a family's time and money are spent on pets at the expense of children or elderly parents, it may cause resentment, and decisions about medical care or inheritance become confusing. Admittedly, pets are important to many people, especially those who live alone, and the grief at losing one can be genuine and deep. Some therapy animals even help to treat anxiety and loneliness. This importance deserves respect, but it differs in kind from the relationships between people. A balanced view recognises pets as valued companions and family members as irreplaceable.

In conclusion, I disagree that pets are as important as family members, because they cannot offer the same relationships or obligations, although they enrich many lives.

89.text:
In many developed countries, the average woman now has fewer than two children, and some governments worry about shrinking populations. This essay will analyse the principal causes of low birth rates and propose realistic solutions.

Low birth rates reflect the high cost of raising children and the difficulty of combining work and family. Housing, childcare and education are expensive, women increasingly pursue careers and marry later, and long working hours and insecure jobs make couples delay or limit families. A couple who postpone parenthood until they can afford a larger flat, for example, may find that they have only one child. In addition, changes in attitudes, such as greater emphasis on personal freedom and careers, and access to contraception, mean that parenthood is a choice made later and less often than in the past. Concern about the future, including climate change and economic uncertainty, also discourages some couples. As a result, many people end up with fewer children than they would like.

To address this issue, governments should make it easier for couples to have the children they want. Affordable childcare, housing support, parental leave for both parents, flexible working and financial help reduce the costs and career penalties of having a child. In addition, employers can be encouraged to offer part-time options and to avoid penalising workers who take leave. Countries that have introduced generous and well-designed family policies, such as in parts of northern Europe, have generally seen higher birth rates than those that have not. Immigration can also help to maintain the workforce, although it is not a complete solution on its own.

In conclusion, low birth rates stem mainly from the costs of raising children and the difficulty of balancing work and family, but practical support for parents offers a realistic way forward.

Ví dụ cặp hoãn làm cha mẹ cho đến khi mua được căn hộ lớn chỉ có một con. Thái độ thay đổi, tránh thai; lo lắng tương lai (khí hậu, kinh tế).

97.text:
The first few years of life shape a child's health, learning and behaviour for decades, and many governments now invest in nurseries and early education. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on early childhood care: better outcomes for children and wider gains for families and the economy.

First and foremost, good care in the early years gives children a lasting advantage. The brain develops fastest before the age of five, and quality nurseries build language, social skills and curiosity. A child who spends mornings in a good nursery, for example, enters school already able to listen, share and speak in sentences. Children from disadvantaged homes benefit most, since they may have fewer books and less conversation at home, so early care narrows the gap before formal schooling starts. As a result, children arrive at school ready to learn, and they are less likely to need extra support or to drop out later. Trained staff can also notice health or developmental problems early.

In addition, early childhood care brings wider benefits to families and the economy. When affordable care is available, parents, especially mothers, can return to work, which raises household income and tax revenue and supports gender equality. Research in several countries has found that every unit of money spent on high-quality early education returns several times as much through better school results, higher earnings and lower costs for health, welfare and crime. Although high-quality care requires investment in staff training and buildings, and poor-quality care can do little good, the long-term returns are large. Countries such as Denmark and Sweden, where early care is widely available and highly regarded, show how a society can benefit.

To sum up, early childhood care brings clear benefits to a country, above all better outcomes for children and wider economic gains. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

111.text:
Many countries face two demographic pressures at once: young families need help to raise children, while the number of very old people is growing quickly. This is why opinions are divided as to whether public money should be focused on childcare or on elder care. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of childcare argue that it invests in the future and lets parents work. Good care in the early years builds language, social skills and curiosity, helping children to do well at school and later in life. A child who spends mornings in a good nursery, for example, enters school already able to listen, share and speak in sentences. When affordable care is available, parents, especially mothers, can return to work, which raises household income and tax revenue. The returns on early investment are large, since healthier, better-educated children become productive adults who will support future generations.

On the other hand, supporters of elder care point out that older people have often worked and paid taxes for decades and deserve dignity in their final years. Many suffer from frailty, dementia or loneliness, and without care they may be neglected, while their relatives are forced to cut their working hours. A woman who looks after both her young children and her elderly mother, for example, may be forced to give up her job. With populations ageing, the demand for care is growing fast, and failure to meet it would cause great suffering.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that a balanced budget is wise, with childcare given priority where early investment is most lacking, while elder care is expanded in line with the growth of the ageing population.

123.text:
When a child does well at school, parents often receive some of the credit, and when a child struggles, they sometimes receive the blame. This essay will explain two key ways in which parents influence children's academic success: through encouragement and routine, and through the resources and expectations that they provide.

First and foremost, parents shape children's academic success through encouragement, routine and interest. Children whose parents read with them, set regular times for homework and show curiosity about school tend to achieve more. A parent who sits with a child for twenty minutes of homework every evening, for example, shows that learning matters, and the child sees study as a normal part of life. Praise for effort rather than just results builds confidence and persistence, and a calm home with enough sleep and breakfast supports concentration. Talking to children about books, news and ideas also develops vocabulary and curiosity long before they start school.

In addition, parents provide resources and set expectations. They can buy books, find a quiet place to study, arrange tutors or help with school choices, and they communicate with teachers when problems arise. Realistic expectations motivate children, since young people often try to live up to what their parents believe they can do. However, excessive pressure can have the opposite effect, causing stress, anxiety and a dislike of learning. Parents are also not the only influence, as teachers, friends and the child's own character matter, and children from poorer families may succeed with the help of good schools and committed teachers. Support works better than pressure, and parents should show interest and encouragement rather than demanding top marks.

To sum up, parents play an important role in children's academic success by providing encouragement, structure and resources, provided that they avoid excessive pressure. For these reasons, their involvement should be welcomed.

146.text:
Many children now receive a smartphone before they start secondary school, and some argue that children should not use smartphones at all. I agree to a large extent, since young children are not ready for unrestricted phones, although complete bans are neither realistic nor always desirable for older children.

To begin with, young children are not ready for unrestricted smartphones. Phones distract from schoolwork, disturb sleep, expose children to unsuitable content and online bullying, and replace play and exercise, although they allow parents and children to stay in contact. A ten-year-old who scrolls on a phone in bed until midnight, for example, arrives at school tired and distracted. Studies have linked heavy use among young people to anxiety, low mood and poor sleep, and games and social media are designed to hold attention for as long as possible. Children also lack the judgment to deal with strangers, advertising and pressure to share personal images, and they may not tell adults when something goes wrong.

Furthermore, childhood is a time for activities that phones can replace, such as outdoor play, reading, face-to-face friendship and hobbies. Delaying and limiting use protects health, learning and development. However, a complete ban has drawbacks. Phones can keep children safe by allowing them to call parents, and as they grow older they need to learn how to use technology responsibly, since it is part of modern life. A sensible approach would give young children a basic phone, if any, set clear rules about when and where phones are used, and allow smartphones gradually, with parental controls and conversations about safety, from around the early teens.

In conclusion, children should not use smartphones freely, particularly when young, because of the risks to health and learning, but supervised and limited use as they mature is reasonable.

Ví dụ đứa trẻ mười tuổi lướt điện thoại trên giường đến nửa đêm đến trường mệt và xao nhãng. Nghiên cứu liên hệ dùng nhiều với lo âu, tâm trạng thấp, ngủ kém; trò chơi và mạng xã hội thiết kế để giữ chú ý; trẻ thiếu phán đoán với người lạ, quảng cáo, áp lực chia sẻ ảnh cá nhân.

Tuổi thơ là lúc chơi ngoài trời, đọc sách, tình bạn trực tiếp, sở thích; trì hoãn và giới hạn bảo vệ sức khoẻ, học tập. Trẻ không nên dùng tự do nhất là khi nhỏ; dùng có giám sát, giới hạn khi lớn lên là hợp lý.

176.text:
Every year, thousands of people spend weeks or months working without pay in distant countries, from building schools to teaching English, and the benefits of volunteering abroad are often discussed. This essay will explain two key ways in which volunteering abroad benefits communities and volunteers: by meeting real needs and by promoting learning and understanding.

First and foremost, volunteering abroad can help communities if it matches local needs. Volunteers with skills such as teaching or medicine fill real gaps and can bring knowledge, energy and extra hands to projects with limited funds. A volunteer who teaches English in a village for six months, for example, may help children to learn, but unless the project is planned, she may leave before it can continue. When projects are led by local people and organisations, the benefit lasts, because volunteers support community priorities rather than imposing their own. Volunteers can also raise funds and awareness back at home, bringing wider attention to local problems.

In addition, volunteers gain a great deal. They learn about other cultures and ways of life, develop language and practical skills, and often return with greater confidence, maturity and a wish to continue helping. Contact between people from different countries can reduce prejudice and build friendships across borders. However, there are risks. Short, poorly planned visits may take work from local people, create dependence or provide little real help, and volunteers without training can cause harm, for example in orphanages or clinics. Organisations should therefore select volunteers carefully, train them, work with local partners and measure results. Choosing reputable programmes is important for anyone who wants their time to make a difference.

To sum up, volunteering abroad benefits communities and volunteers when it meets local needs and is well organised. For these reasons, it deserves support, but only in responsible forms.

Ví dụ người dạy tiếng Anh sáu tháng ở làng có thể giúp trẻ nhưng nếu không có kế hoạch sẽ rời đi trước khi dự án tiếp tục. Có lợi khi đáp ứng nhu cầu địa phương và tổ chức tốt; nên ủng hộ nhưng chỉ dạng có trách nhiệm.

192.text:
Charities, schools and neighbourhood groups depend on people who give their time freely, and opinions differ on whether individuals should be responsible for volunteering or whether society and government should encourage it. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of personal responsibility argue that volunteering depends on personal motivation. People volunteer when they care about a cause, and a gift of time is valuable precisely because it is freely given. Forcing or pressuring people may produce half-hearted effort and resentment, and a person who is made to volunteer may not value the work. A resident who chooses to help clean a river because she loves the place, for example, is likely to work harder and keep going longer than someone who is told to do so. Voluntary service also reflects a healthy civil society in which citizens, not officials, take the initiative to solve problems.

On the other hand, supporters of public encouragement point out that many people would volunteer if it were made easier. Schools can offer course credit for community service, employers can provide paid time off, and governments can fund volunteer organisations, provide training and recognise the work with awards or tax benefits. Many people do not volunteer simply because they do not know how to start or cannot spare the time. Such support does not remove the voluntary element, but it opens opportunities, especially for young people and those from poorer backgrounds who might not otherwise get involved. Well-run organisations also ensure that volunteers' time is used effectively.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that volunteering should remain a personal choice, but governments, schools and employers should make it easier and more rewarding through practical support.

Tình nguyện phụ thuộc động cơ cá nhân: người ta làm khi quan tâm; tặng thời gian có giá trị vì tự nguyện; ép buộc gây nỗ lực nửa vời, bực bội. Ví dụ cư dân tự chọn dọn sông vì yêu nơi đó làm chăm hơn người bị bảo làm. Phản ánh xã hội dân sự lành mạnh nơi công dân tự chủ động.

plan.think: Nhiều người sẽ tình nguyện nếu dễ hơn: trường cho điểm quá trình, nhà tuyển dụng cho nghỉ phép có lương, chính phủ tài trợ tổ chức, đào tạo, ghi nhận bằng giải thưởng hoặc ưu đãi thuế; nhiều người không biết bắt đầu hoặc không có thời gian; mở cơ hội cho người trẻ và nghèo; tổ chức tốt dùng thời gian hiệu quả.
Giữ là lựa chọn cá nhân nhưng chính phủ, trường, nhà tuyển dụng hỗ trợ thực tế.

196.text:
Every family has its own habits, from the way birthdays are celebrated to the stories told at dinner, and these shared customs shape how people see themselves. This essay will explain two key ways in which family traditions influence identity: by giving a sense of belonging and by passing on values and memories.

First and foremost, family traditions give children a sense of belonging and identity. Shared rituals such as festival meals, religious ceremonies and annual trips create a feeling of being part of a group with its own history. A family that cooks the same festival dish together every year, for example, creates memories that tie generations together. Children who take part know that they are connected to people before them and after them, which gives them security and a stable starting point from which to explore the world. Even simple customs, such as a weekly Sunday lunch, can make a child feel that he or she belongs.

In addition, traditions pass on values and cultural heritage. Through stories, songs and customs, grandparents and parents teach respect, generosity, honesty and the history of the family or community, often without formal lessons. Language, food and festivals link people to their culture, which matters particularly for families who have moved to another country. However, traditions can also restrict individual choice if they are applied rigidly, for example when young people feel pressured to follow a career or marriage that their family expects. Healthy traditions are flexible, allowing new generations to adapt them and to add their own. Identity then grows from a balance between inherited roots and personal choice.

To sum up, family traditions strongly influence identity by giving belonging and passing on values, provided that they allow room for individual development. For these reasons, they deserve to be valued and kept alive.

plan.think: Mở bài nêu thói quen riêng của mỗi gia đình (cách mừng sinh nhật, câu chuyện kể bên bữa ăn) định hình cách người ta nhìn mình; báo hai cách: cảm giác thuộc về; truyền giá trị và ký ức.

Nghi lễ chung (bữa tiệc lễ, nghi thức tôn giáo, chuyến đi hằng năm) tạo cảm giác thuộc về nhóm có lịch sử riêng. Ví dụ gia đình nấu cùng một món lễ mỗi năm tạo ký ức gắn các thế hệ. Trẻ biết mình nối với người trước và sau, có an toàn và điểm xuất phát ổn định; phong tục đơn giản như bữa trưa Chủ nhật cũng làm trẻ thấy thuộc về.

Giới hạn: truyền thống cứng nhắc hạn chế lựa chọn cá nhân (nghề, hôn nhân gia đình kỳ vọng); truyền thống lành mạnh linh hoạt cho thế hệ mới thích nghi.

203.text:
In many families, grandparents collect children from school, cook meals and tell stories, and they are an important part of how children grow up. This essay will explain two key roles that grandparents play in child upbringing: providing care and stability, and passing on values and a link with the past.

First and foremost, grandparents provide care, stability and emotional security. They look after grandchildren while parents work, which saves families money and gives working parents peace of mind. In some countries, grandparents provide a large share of childcare, and in households with a single parent or two jobs, their help can be essential. A grandparent in good health, for example, can help to look after grandchildren and pass on knowledge, which supports working parents. Children also gain from the patience and attention that grandparents often have time to give, and from having another adult who loves them unconditionally and who can be a refuge when there are tensions at home.

In addition, grandparents pass on values, stories and skills. A grandmother who tells stories about her childhood, for example, gives a child a living link with history, and grandparents often teach traditions, language, cooking, crafts and manners. This helps children to understand their roots and to respect older people. However, there are some difficulties. Grandparents may have different ideas about discipline, sweets or screen time, which can cause conflict with parents, and their own health or energy may limit what they can do. Clear communication between generations, and respect for the parents' final say, usually resolve such disagreements. Where possible, children should also be encouraged to contribute to the relationship, for instance by helping grandparents with technology.

To sum up, grandparents play a valuable role in child upbringing by providing care and by passing on values and heritage. For these reasons, their contribution should be recognised and supported.

plan.step: 2. Vai trò 1 — chăm sóc, ổn định
plan.think: Chăm cháu khi cha mẹ đi làm: tiết kiệm tiền, cha mẹ yên tâm; ở nhiều nước ông bà chăm trẻ phần lớn, gia đình đơn thân hoặc hai việc cần giúp. Ví dụ ông bà khoẻ giúp chăm cháu và truyền kiến thức hỗ trợ cha mẹ đi làm. Trẻ được kiên nhẫn, sự chú ý; người lớn yêu vô điều kiện; nơi nương tựa khi căng thẳng ở nhà.

plan.step: 3. Vai trò 2 — giá trị, kỹ năng + khó khăn

Khó khăn: khác ý về kỷ luật, đồ ngọt, thời gian màn hình gây xung đột với cha mẹ; sức khoẻ, sức lực hạn chế; giao tiếp rõ và tôn trọng quyền quyết định cuối của cha mẹ.
Vai trò đáng giá; cần được ghi nhận và hỗ trợ.
